During my traveling years, I stopped off in Korea on my way home from China. My father’s youngest brother—작은아버지, who was 53 at the time—met me in downtown Seoul and showed me around the city - specifically 경복궁.

As we walked through the grand courtyards of Gyeongbokgung, the main palace, we shared a realization: despite all the elaborately painted timber and sprawling stone grounds, our lives were undeniably better than those of the Joseon dynasty kings.

At the time, Korea’s per capita GDP stood around \$12,841. In the years since, that number has nearly tripled to over \$37,000.

Even after accounting for inflation, the real growth of the nation has more than doubled.

If we had a richer life than kings then, we were living like deities compared to the post-war period—enjoying health, warmth, mobility, and comfort that no Koreans ever enjoyed, neither ancient nor recent.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

The stone walls of Seoul's royal palaces once kept the world out, preserving luxury for a select few.

It is estimated roughly 39,000 visitors are experiencing the palaces built, burned and rebuilt.

Today, withnessing the vibrant, modern city, you realize the greatest achievement is not what is preserved inside—for it can be reconstructed. It is the fact that the people of Korea sacrificed, fought and built the nation that is often called the Economic Miracle.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Author Jim Collins in his book, Built to Last covers a concept that he called, Preserve the Core and expand.

That is what Korea managed to do.

They preserved the past and made future possible.

Now the world agrees with its approach and confirms by visiting the nation by the millions.
